subtopic: U.S. TARIFF ON CANADIAN CEDAR SHAKES AND SHINGLES- GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
U.S. TARIFF ON CANADIAN CEDAR SHAKES AND SHINGLES- GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 22, the United States Government moved without prior notice to protect American shakes and shingles producers by imposing a 35 per cent duty on imported shakes and shingles. This action was taken in full knowledge that Canadian producers were competing fairly, without subsidy, and that a major factor in the decline of the American industry was a lack of red cedar logs.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated, the Canadian Government finds this action unjustified and unacceptable. It flies in the face of past commitments to refrain from discretionary protectionist actions and to consult in such situations.

It runs counter to current attempts to liberalize trade between our two countries.

We have made a determined effort to regain full access to the U.S. market and we will continue those efforts. At the same time, over the past few days, the Government has examined its legal options for redress. As is customary under international practice, we have approached the United States Government to find out whether it was prepared to remove the restriction, or to offer compensation to redress the imbalance in conditions of trade caused by the United States' action.

The U.S. administration has made it clear that it is not prepared to remove the measure, to compensate Canada or to take other measures to ensure that Canadian shakes and shingles manufacturers maintain reasonable access to the U.S. market.

In the circumstances, we have decided reluctantly that an appropriate and measured response is required now. Our objective is to bring home to the United States the costs of protectionism, while avoiding measures which will only worsen our own situation.
The Government will implement the following measures which will take effect on June 6, the effective date of the United States' tariff increase on cedar shakes and shingles.
First, on a number of tariff items relating to certain books, certain periodicals and other publications, Canada for several years has allowed duty-free entry. The rates that would otherwise apply for the most important items are at a maximum of 10 per cent. Nearly 90 per cent, or approximately $360 million of Canada's imports under these tariff items in 1985, originated in the United States.
We eliminated the duty on these items on the understanding that the United States would exempt Canada from the
Statements by Ministers
application of the so-called United States manufacturing clause of the U.S. Copyright Act. This provision of United States law requires that any material written by a U.S. national or resident must be printed in the United States to benefit from U.S. copyright protection. As a result of complaints from the European Community, the manufacturing clause has been found by the GATT to be inconsistent with the United States' GATT obligations.
In these circumstances, the Government will be moving to restore the tariff items in question to their previous levels, effective June 6. The reimposition of the rate of duty will result in the collection of about $36 million in additional duties. I see no reason why we should continue to provide compensation for relief from a measure that was wrongfully imposed.
I should note that the U.S. legislative authority for the manufacturing clause expires at the end of June this year and that, given the GATT finding, the administration would be expected to veto any proposed extension. However, should it be extended, we will join with the EEC in pressing for compensation. Should it not be extended, we will seek other ways to ensure the integrity of our response to the U.S. action on shakes and shingles.
Second, the Government will reimpose duties on computer parts imports and on imports of semi-conductors of types made in Canada. At the United States' urging, Canada recently joined a trilateral agreement with that country and Japan to allow duty-free entry of such goods. Import values of these goods from the United States are very high. By withdrawing from that agreement and by reimposing the rates of duty which previously applied, $41 million in extra revenues from the United States imports would result.
Third, there is also a range of other unbound products in which the trade is not large but which, if duties on them were raised, would make clear to the U.S. administration, the Congress and various interest groups, however small, that yielding to protectionist pressure is not without cost. These rates are being raised.
To give effect to these tariff rate increases, I have just tabled a notice of Ways and Means. Amendments will be introduced to legislation currently before Parliament and the necessary recommendations will be made to Governor in Council to ensure that all the actions in our response to the United States tariff become effective on June 6.

The government takes no pleasure in implementing these actions.

But legitimate Canadian interests must be protected and nations which resort to unjustified protectionism must be made to realize that trade is a two-way street.
As Hon. Members know, Government representatives met last week with management and labour representatives of the

June 2, 1986
Statements by Ministers
shakes and shingles industry who are aware of our concern and our effort to restore normal access to the U.S. market for their products. We intend, as of June 6 when the United States' measure takes effect, to monitor closely its impact on Canadian exports. We will meet with industry representatives shortly thereafter to assess the impact and decide what measures might be necessary and appropriate to assist the industry to adjust. There are those who suggest that this American action provides sufficient cause to suspend or even to cancel the overall Canada-United States trade negotiations. We must not heed this counsel of despair. The shakes and shingles incident underlines the need for us to persist in our efforts to secure and enhance our access to the U.S. market.
There are also those who seek to link the shakes and shingles dispute with the ongoing issue of softwood lumber exports to the United States. They will try to make the case that our response to the shakes and shingles dispute will precipitate a U.S. decision to launch a countervailing duty investigation into Canadian softwood lumber exports. There is simply no basis for linking the two issues. I believe it is important for Hon. Members to recognize the fundamental difference between the two issues. On the one hand, the recent 35 per cent duty on shakes and shingles was imposed by the U.S. administration to protect an industry unable to compete with fairly traded imports. It was a blatant protectionist act. On the other hand, the softwood lumber case is one of a number of cases involving a complaint that Canadian producers are competing unfairly in the American market.
We reject the allegation of unfair subsidy, just as the appropriate American tribunal rejected the same charge in 1983. We will, therefore, continue to challenge the right of American lobby groups to harass Canadian producers with the same charge of subsidization. We are confident that Canadian producers will ultimately be vindicated should they be subjected to double jeopardy in American trade tribunals. I should add that there are other Canadian products facing allegations of unfair trade practices and we will be watching developments in those cases very closely.

Mr. Speaker, I have today outlined the Canadian response to this unhappy event. It is a measured response-one that recognizes that a trade war between Canada and the United States would serve no useful purpose.

We have long said that trade means jobs, not only for Canadians but for Americans as well. It is our hope that with these actions, our two countries can begin to put this unfortunate episode behind us and get on with the job of ensuring greater certainly and stability in the relationship so that trade can continue freely and fairly between our two countries.

subtopic: U.S. TARIFF ON CANADIAN CEDAR SHAKES AND SHINGLES- GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising in response to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), I want first to express two notes of sympathy. My sympathy goes to the over 4,000 workers in British Columbia who have been given absolutely nothing today by the Government of Canada. They are the ones for whom we must really feel sorry. They have been abandoned by their Government and left out to hang by the lack of any effective or useful response. Second, I must express my sympathy to the Minister of Finance who, once again, has been the sacrificial lamb for his Government after the keystone cops who put this whole process into place abandoned him, leaving him to "rag the puck" as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri- Westmount (Mr. Johnston), said the other day. He said the Minister of Finance was sent out as a penalty killer. I suggest there is another definition. He will now be widely known throughout the land as the "mouse that roared". The only difference is that the present Minister of Finance has succeeded in making the late Peter Sellers look like a sobersides statesman by comparison.
One can only ridicule and laugh at the measures brought forward today as the so-called "tough response" which was promised 10 days ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Minister has referred to an "unfortunate episode". All along the Government has said this is a "singular accident", it is only something which is isolated in the American mind. Yet this afternoon we have a report from Washington that the United States has now imposed the ruling of the International Trade Commission, a 41 per cent tariff on Canadian imports of steel related to the gas and oil manufacturing industry. So much for the isolated incident. The people in the riding of the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and in Regina will now face the full vent of another American action, again prompted by its sense that it knows this Government will not respond in a tough, effective way.
The Prime Minister once said: "If the winds of protectionism ever blow over Canada, they can cut me up into little pieces". The pieces are scattered all over the floor. The Prime Minister has been cut to pieces by his so-called close friend, the American President.
This is not an effective reaction to an isolated incident. It is a consistent, coherent strategy on the part of the United States to impose a series of trade reactions against this country, obviously prompted by the fact the Americans have seen a group of pussycats in the Conservative Government who have not been able to win American respect because they have given up and conceded on everything else up until now.
The Government is going to be very brave. It is going to reimpose a tariff on books and publications, except that there is a little caveat which says "until the end of June". That is 24 days of tough action. That is really going to have President Reagan shaking and shingling in his boots. After 24 days it may not matter any more. Furthermore, the Government is going to impose a whole new set of tariffs. It is really going to get after a lot of people. There will be a new tariff on porridge, on Christmas trees and on tea. It is bad enough that it is putting 4,000 people out of work in British Columbia but now
June 2, 1986

they will not even be able to enjoy Christmas, their kids will not have their porridge and their grandmothers will not be able to drink their tea without paying a higher cost. This is the Brave New World of this Government, and that is the end result of what it is doing.
How could anyone take this action seriously? How could anyone accept that this will provide the appropriate response from the Americans so they will say: "Oh, boy, those Canadians can really get tough when they want to"? The Government is going to put a little more tax on rolled oats. Our horses and those who want a little gruel in the morning are going to have to pay a higher cost for it.
Another very brilliant stroke of genius on the part of the Minister and his Government is to reimpose a tariff it just took off in January on computer parts. The Government is always talking about the need for more productivity, the need to be more competitive and to be able to provide a higher level of efficiency in that industry. But what does it do now to Canadian manufacturers? It will impose a tariff on a range of computer parts which are necessary to keep the manufacturers going. And it is going to review that again. So no one knows what the Government is doing. Everyone is full of uncertainty.
In the meantime, what about the workers? What about those people who demonstrated last weekend to save their jobs? We have asked all along why the Prime Minister does not use his so-called vaunted special relationship with the President of the United States. He has worked 15 months at the job. He said: "I alone am able to provide for an open sesame to the White House". But the first time that is tested, the very first time Canadians depend upon the Prime Minister to pick up the telephone and open up a special line of communication with the President, he is afraid and will not do so. After 15 months of giving away on FIRA, the NEP, pharmaceuticals and publications, all those matters of importance to this country, at the very time we should call in our chips, what does the Prime Minister do?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EQUALITY RIGHTS ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING SUBCOMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATIONS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EQUALITY RIGHTS ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING SUBCOMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should implement the recommendations of the subcommittee on equality rights of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs:
(1)	That all trades and occupations in the Canadian Armed Forces be opened to women.
(2)	That Canadian Armed Forces practices relating to the employment and promotion of women be monitored by the Canadian Human Rights Commission and that progress in revising policies in the manner we recommend be evaluated by the Commission at regular intervals.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to rise to participate today in the debate on an important motion respecting the rights of Canadian women. On April 17 of last year, Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms came into effect. That section ensured equality for all Canadians and put an end to discrimination on the basis of sex. However, there is one major bastion which remains within the federal Public Service that quite explicitly continues to discriminate against women, that is, the Canadian Armed Forces.
Effectively the motion before the House today reiterates the unanimous recommendation of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights on which I had the honour to serve as a member. That committee heard representations from women within the Armed Forces and outside the Armed Forces from right across Canada in respect of the role of women and the doors which remained closed to women within the Armed Forces. We heard very clearly a sense of common concern that our overriding objective as Canadians clearly must be the pursuit of peace and putting an end to the madness of war. As well, I believe it is very important to recognize the fundamental right of conscientious objection. Those people who feel through deep personal belief that they are unable or unwilling to serve in time of war or time of combat should have the right to exercise that through conscientious objection. As members of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights we heard from many women who wanted an opportunity to serve at all levels within the Canadian Armed Forces, women who are currently denied that right. I should like to give a couple of examples of the effect of this discrimination.

June 2, 1986
Equality Rights
For example, we heard from a woman named Linda Long who has been associated with the military for more than 10 years of regular and reserve forces service. She said:
I am a military woman, I am loyal to the service, the service I still love-The reason 1 came is my depth of love for my military service and my feeling that a disservice was being done to my personal tradition in uniform and to those honourable women who yet are serving and cannot speak for themselves.
They cannot speak for themselves because unfortunately the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) issued an edict which effectively denied Canadian military women the right to appear before our committee and testify in respect of conditions within the Armed Forces. It was with a feeling of pride in the Armed Forces, tempered by a sense of anger in the face of such blatant unfairness, that a number of former service women described to the committee the treatment of women by the Department of National Defence. Colonel Shirley Robinson, who deserves credit for having put a tremendous amount of energy and dedication into this question after having served in the Canadian Armed Forces for more than 30 years, set it out very clearly in her submission to the committee. She said:
If the Canadian Forces gain exemption from the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, a dangerous precedent will be set; for it will signal to the people of Canada that women can continue to be excluded from certain employment simply because men don't want them there. For that really is the bottom line, isn't it? And all the arguments, excuses and blame directed against women have been built upon this appalling fact. The fulfilment of our military requirements rests on the creation of an armed force adequately endowed with the necessary person power and technological skills; and motivated by the belief that the military establishment embodies the values of society from which it originates.
She concludes by saying:
Equal employment opportunities for military women are much more compatible with this objective than the preservation of a backwards, machismo ethos.
That sets it out very clearly, Mr. Speaker. At the present time, over 70,000 jobs within the Canadian Armed Forces are effectively denied to women. The rationale for this is completely unacceptable. It all boils down in most cases to a suggestion that women as a group are somehow inferior to men and unable to serve with distinction in the Canadian Armed Forces. Of course, this is the antithesis of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms because the Charter of Rights and Freedoms requires that people be judged as individuals, and there is no doubt whatever that there are many individual Canadian women who are quite able to meet the most rigorous qualifications for the Canadian Armed Forces in every sense.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission has recently asked the President of the Human Rights Tribunal panel to appoint an independent tribunal to look into the Department of National Defence's policy of excluding women from combat positions. One of the examples given in this area is a women from Valleyfield, Quebec, who was refused entry into a DND sponsored course for naval mechanics solely on the basis of her sex. Not only did the Subcommittee on Equality Rights make strong recommendations with respect to this matter, but the Canadian Human Rights Commission itself has launched an investigation. As long ago as 1971 the Royal Commission on
the Status of Women recommended that all trades and occupations be open to women.
The Government, on March 4 of this year, responded to the unanimous recommendations of the Equality Rights Subcommittee, but it appears that once again the male generals, because of course there are no female generals, are attempting to sabotage equality within the Canadian Armed Forces. They are using delaying tactics and weasel words. What do they say, Mr. Speaker? They say that this must be done in a way-and no one can disagree-that is compatible with operational effectiveness within the Canadian Forces. They say that there is a conflict between operational effectiveness and equality and that one must not yield to the other. That is simply not true. Equality for women within the Canadian Armed Forces can be achieved at the same time as full operational effectiveness is guaranteed.
The group that has been working long and hard to promote full equality within the Canadian Armed Forces, a group known as the Association for Women's Equity in the Canadian Forces, has made a number of specific recommendations in this area. It acknowledges that the number one priority of the forces must be to maintain operational effectiveness. The group points out that operational effectiveness would not in any way be jeopardized by the introduction of women into all occupations as long as the introduction is done in a manner which is informed, fair and efficient. They point out the need for a change in attitudes and for education, particularly among senior male personnel within the Department of National Defence.
The association recommends leadership training programs and calls as well for the establishment of an external review process which would involve perhaps former members of the Canadian Armed Forces. As well, review and redrafting must be undertaken of all policies and practices prejudicial against service women. An example of that is the current policy to accord women leave without pay with the associated loss of benefits and seniority rather than sick leave during the period when a servicewomen is unfit for duty during and after pregnancy. This is blatantly unfair to women who become pregnant while in the Armed Forces, and certainly that is one of the areas that is a denial of equality as well. There must be selection standards and procedures that are based on bona fide occupational requirements. Obviously there must be a recognition of the concept of reasonable accommodation as well.
Monitoring by an outside independent body of experts is essential to ensure that the Armed Forces do not delay in the implementation of full equality. The committee has noted that there is an excellent precedent for this with the Defence Advisory Committee on Women and the Services in the United States.
I want to note as well that while the Government has made a commitment on paper, that commitment falls far short of action. General McLellan has been asked to undertake a review of this commitment, and there is to be further delay
June 2, 1986

while yet another task force studies the matter. Because I have a very short time to promote this motion, let me conclude by once again recognizing, as Adell Karmas pointed out very eloquently:
War is terrible and loathsome. No one truly wants to be part of war and the bloodshed and misery it entails, but the reality is people fight to protect a country, a system of beliefs, a valued way of life.
It is insulting to all Canadian women that they are denied the right to participate fully in all trades and occupations in the Canadian Armed Forces.
I call upon the Government to accept in reality, not just on paper, the important recommendation that all trades and occupations be open to women and the implementation of this important principle be monitored by an external review agency. Equality must come at last to the Canadian Armed Forces.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EQUALITY RIGHTS ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING SUBCOMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity for the House to debate this issue, partly because of its significance in principle. If it were just a matter of principle, I think I would want to support the motion. As one who cast his vote to open up a formerly all male profession to give women an opportunity to enter it, as one who had a leadership role in opening up an all male college to become a co-ed institution, I could welcome the opportunity for taking an advance in the direction this motion calls.
I am more impressed that this is a matter of practice, and ironically were we to adopt this motion and put it into practice it might work counter to the interests of the very people for whom the Hon. Member is seeking to be an advocate, and rightly so. I think the focus of our attention should not be the theoretical consideration, important as that may be in certain circumstances, but, rather, the practical effect that this motion could have on the women who would want to participate in the Armed Forces and advance their careers in the military. I am going to suggest that, ironically, were we to adopt this motion we would work against the interests of the very women whose interests we seek to serve.
Let us recognize that right now Canada has a very impressive record in terms of making the military service accessible to women. Canada has the third highest ratio of women in its Armed Forces, with 8.9 per cent of the full-time professional personnel of the Canadian Armed Forces being women. Israel has 10 per cent and the United States 9.5 per cent. We are close behind. The United Kingdom is a distant fourth with 5.1 per cent and Belgium with 3.8 per cent. Our record is impressive and we have nothing to apologize for. As well, we can take encouragement from the way in which the Canadian Armed Forces over the past 15 years have steadily increased the positions open to women, the percentage growing from 19 per cent to 65 per cent, 29,000 positions now being opened to women candidates.
If we were to move beyond the present policy and make mandatory as a matter of policy the unlimited deployment of women in all positions in the Armed forces, we might well find
Equality Rights
that the unintentional result was the reduction of the percentage of women in the Armed Forces. That has been perhaps the result of certain countries practising unlimited deployment. For example, of the three countries that practise unlimited deployment of women in their Armed Forces, each one is well behind Canada in the proportion of women in its armed personnel: Belgium with 3.8 per cent, the Netherlands with 1.4 per cent and Norway with 1.2 per cent. As well, those countries have few women in what the Canadian Armed Forces would call combat roles. When we speak of those three countries permitting women to undertake combat service we may conjure up images of rows and rows of female regiments and divisions, but that is not the case. There are only 18 to 30 in actual combat roles in those countries, with another 65 serving actively with combat units having non-combat roles. It is also significant that some countries which had women in combat service in the past, including Israel, Yugoslavia, and the Soviet Union, have withdrawn that policy.
We must consider very seriously the practical implications of what this motion recommends. We must recognize that Canada now has a larger percentage of women in its Armed Forces than have any of the countries which practise unlimited deployment. The actual implementation of deploying women in combat roles in those countries is very limited with regard to the numbers concerned. According to our present policies, we are actually giving women far more opportunities to serve their country in the military than are the other countries which I have mentioned.
If we were to change courses radically and admit women to all roles including combat roles, the unintentional result might be to reduce the number of women in our Armed Forces. One reason for that is that they would have to meet the same medical standards imposed upon men in combat service. It is estimated by some experts in the field that this could reduce the number of women in our Armed Forces to 2 per cent, which is far below the present ratio.
I would hope, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that in the interest of women we would give priority to the practical implications of this motion. We should increase opportunities for women in the military by continuing with the present policy and, in keeping with the Charter of Rights, studying the various positions which are presently closed to women candidates to discover how many can be opened to them. As well, we should give priority to advancing women within the ranks of the Armed Forces. There are presently no women generals. That is a lack which we would want to make up for at the earliest opportunity. As soon as a position is open for which a woman is eligible we should give that promotion priority.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to add a few comments to this debate on the motion before the House. This is a motion to open all of the occupations and trades in the Canadian Armed Forces, particularly those of a combat nature, to women. I cannot help but wonder why anyone would want to enter into a combat role. Surely our prime objective is to ensure that neither males nor females would have to fight in a war. I do not know why anyone wants to get involved in this in the first place.
I would like to comment specifically on some of the points contained in this motion. We must use a large measure of common sense and pay attention to the basic principles of the Armed Forces when discussing this motion. What in the world do the Armed Forces exist for in the first place? They are not there to provide employment opportunities or to be in the forefront of social change. They are not there to hold little sensitivity groups talking about human rights. The purpose of the Armed Forces is to be there with one single, over-riding objective, that being to protect the security and sovereignty of Canada and to protect the rights and freedoms enjoyed by all Canadians. Everything the Armed Forces does must be directly related to that one over-riding objective. Therefore, we
must ensure that all of the trades and occupations within the Armed Forces serve that one over-riding objective.
Whenever a trade or occupation can be open equally to men and women, we obviously want to do that, as the Canadian Armed Forces are doing today. That is what the Government is committed to. The Government is committed to expanding the role of women in the Armed Forces by ensuring that women will be able to compete for all of the trades and occupations within the forces. The Government has committed itself to pursuing this policy only in a manner consistent with the requirements of the Armed Forces to be operationally effective in the interests of national security.
We must consider some of the facts. My colleague who just spoke mentioned some of these and I would like to reiterate some of them. Canada is already a leader in the western world in the employment of women in the Armed Forces. Today 8.9 per cent of those employed in the Canadian Armed Forces are women. Of the 29,000 positions open to either men or women, 7,400 are occupied by women. Only two countries in the world have a higher proportion of women in their Armed Forces than does Canada, those being Israel with 10 per cent and the United States with 9.5 per cent. Within the next few years the rate of increase of female trainees will put Canada ahead of some of these other nations.
Constant review within the Armed Forces has resulted in an increase in the proportion of occupations in which women participate from 19 per cent in 1971 to the present 65 per cent, resulting in some 29,000 positions now being available to women. As vacancies occur and suitable applicants become available, there will be considerable scope for expanding the present strength of 7,400 women. As a result of the present Charter of Rights, a task force is studying how to implement that within the Department of National Defence today. The result will be that the number of occupations open to women will undoubtedly increase.
Last fall I was a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence which held hearings across Canada concerning renewal of the NORAD agreement. We listened to briefings from various Armed Forces personnel at bases across Canada. I talked with many officers and they were very interested in the equality report, but their interest focused on two topics. One was sexual orientation in the Armed Forces, and the other was women in combat. On the first point all of the officers I talked to were unanimously opposed to the recommendation to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation. I totally agree with them. On the second point, they were also unanimous that women should never be placed in infantry units or in combat roles where their lack of upper body strength and physical stamina would detract from the mission given to the unit concerned. However, they said that more trades and occupations should be opened to women wherever men and women could compete
June 2, 1986

equally and meet all the qualifications and physical requirements. This is exactly what the Government is doing as I indicated earlier.
I would like to comment now on a fallacy which is argued by some people. It is that all future wars will be push button wars. The experience of the war in the Falklands should teach us some facts. I think that that war clearly indicated that physical fitness and strength was perhaps even more vital than in the past. In the Napoleonic wars, in the early 1800s, Wellington's troops carried packs weighing around 80 pounds. In the Falklands war the British soldier carried a 120-pound pack from San Carlos to Port Stanley. Strength and endurance was as important then, if not more so, than in the past. In that war the world witnessed the terribly destructive force of a small missile when it hit a ship. Once those missiles fired by push buttons hit a ship, physical strength and stamina were as vital as ever to keep the ship afloat and save lives. In that respect we have to pay attention to both common sense and the facts.
Why do the Armed Forces exist in the first place? Whatever the goal of the Armed Forces is, everything that serves to accomplish the goal must be funnelled in that direction. Wherever men and women can serve that goal, fine. Where a lack of physical strength and stamina impede achieving the goal, then that should be the limitation. Where facts tell us otherwise, we have to maintain some measure of objectivity and not allow our feelings or the desire for rights to obliterate common sense completely. We have to let facts teach us. The war in the Falklands clearly suggests that we have to keep physical strength and stamina uppermost in our mind.

to women.
(2)	That Canadian Armed Forces practices relating to the employment and
promotion of women be monitored by the Canadian Human Rights
Equality Rights
Commission and that progress in revising policies in the manner we recommend be evaluated by the Commission at regular intervals.
It was my privilege to serve on the equality rights task force along with six other members of this House. Of the many issues we addressed, the primary one was of blatant discrimination based on sex. As we all well know, that is illegal under Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The law says that people shall be treated equally. It is true that that is qualified for a justifiable reason. There must be an intelligent approach to decision-making, but it cannot be based on sex. It must be based on sound, reasoned arguments.
Before I go further on the question of women in the Armed Forces I must respond to the Hon. Member for Burnaby. I am sure he will agree that women pointed out time and time again during the committee hearings that their interest was in peace. They were against nuclear proliferation. They looked to this world for peace and security for all men and women. The view of most men and women in Canada is that we do not want to have to face the ongoing concern over conflicts around the world. We would like a peaceful world for our children and their children, where respect for differences is such that they are accommodated in a peaceful way, not with armed confrontation. However, it would be unreal for me to say that that is the picture of the world as it exists today. Therefore, as a sovereign nation we have an obligation and a responsibility to protect ourselves with properly equipped Armed Forces. We must participate in world peace-keeping forces and meet our moral and legal commitments to our allies around the world. In doing so we have to look at the world as it is and learn the lessons of history.
What have women been saying about their responsibilities as full partners in this society? The issue of women in combat roles was addressed in 1970 by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. That commission recommended that all trades in the Armed Forces be open to women. After reviewing the recommendation, the forces set out to expand the role of women. The limit involved in a fixed numerical list was removed but employment restrictions were maintained for primary combat roles, remote locations and seagoing service. I know that many of my colleagues across the floor feel that those restrictions should be maintained, but that is not the wish of the women with whom we met. In 1979, the military colleges were open to women. In addition a series of trials were initiated to assess the effect that employment would have on service women in near combat or isolated units putting women into an operational capability. The results of those trials are still not in, but to date the Swinter trials indicate that women met all those obligations in a fine and upstanding manner.
I would like to know how many men would have done so in such difficult circumstances where there were so few women in these large masses and they were being examined through a microscope. I think any one of us would have been very disconcerted and uncomfortable if put in such a situation.

June 2, 1986
Equality Rights
My colleagues across the floor have gone to great lengths to tell us what is happening in other countries of the world, the percentages of who has what in what measure. I could give you all those measurements, all those numbers, all those statistics, but that is not the interest which I have with respect to women's rights and the equal access to job opportunities. The Liberal Party endorses the report's recommendations with respect to women's participation in all trades and all occupations in the Canadian Armed Forces. It is my Party's belief that sexual discrimination within the Armed Forces is unacceptable.
During our committee hearings we were told by the opponents of female participation that there was potential for adverse social and sexual relationships. Such arguments are highly reminiscent of the reasons used formerly to justify keeping women out of the paid workforce, and they were not valid then and they are less so now. What is needed is clear job definition, job description by unbiased leaders who understand how and what the Armed Forces have become in today's society.
I find it astonishing that the arguments on the limitation of the role of women in combat are based on such notions that combat is man's work. This is just the pattern of thinking that our Charter was intended to displace.
We are appalled by the arguments raised which justify sexual discrimination in the Armed Forces. That argument is that a potential enemy may regard mixed forces as less capable. That is completely hypothetical and undeserving of attention.
The problems that commanders, generals and senior army people have, or might have, with the uneven performance is absurd. I would suggest to you that either they are poor managers or they do not recognize that the same kind of uneven and inadequate performance is found in the males who also participate in the Armed Forces. That is a fallacious and specious argument. None of these arguments which they have used in the past are buttressed by evidence, but appear to stem from a bias against women and a desire not to disturb the status quo. I would suggest to you that those are not reasonable undertakings.
We find it astonishing that limitations on the role of women in combat are supposedly based on accepted social and cultural patterns which embrace the idea that combat, as I have said, is strictly a man's job. It is just such patterns of thinking that our Charter, and particularly Section 28, was intended to displace. If cultural acceptance is the litmus test for enforcement of a right, no one has any rights except at the discretion of the majority. That is not what was the intention of our laws of this land. Women are in combat roles in other countries, and they have proven that they can do the job.
I would like to point out that to deny women the right to combat is also to deny them the right to valuable employment opportunities, training and education, and promotion within the Armed Forces. I believe that view is totally unjustifiable
and does not allow women the right as citizens to protect their country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EQUALITY RIGHTS ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING SUBCOMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
I have to say I am surprised and upset by some of the comments made by the Progressive Conservatives in this debate, particularly since the wording of the Private Member's motion of my hon. friend from Burnaby in fact specifically repeats the recommendation which was unanimously put forward by the Subcommittee on Equality Rights, which was endorsed by five Progressive Conservatives, by the Liberal and by the New Democratic Member.
I draw to your attention the regrettable response of the Government which said, first, that it will ensure that women will be able to compete for all trades and occupations. It then undertook to pursue this policy vigorously, but then the weasel words were that it would be done in a manner consistent with the requirement of the Armed Forces to be operationally effective in the interests of national security.
We have heard apologies for the present policies of the Armed Forces, which are in contravention of the Charter, which are not sustained by any legislation, nor by an application before the courts for an exemption. We have heard those apologies from the Government Members, and I would say they do not hold water.
I am not sure whether I would encourage a daughter of mine to take a combat role in the Armed Forces of Canada if she desired to go into the Armed Forces. That is not the issue we are looking for. We are looking at the question of whether women will be treated as a group and stereotyped views, prejudgments will be made about what they should or should not do in the Armed Forces, or whether they should be treated as individuals.
If a woman lacks the necessary strength or other job skills or qualifications for a particular trade or occupation in the Armed Forces then she should not get it. Nobody is saying otherwise. What we are saying is that where a woman wishes to qualify, or take a particular trade, she should not be excluded from that trade because that trade is indirectly linked to combat, as is the case of some 30,000 positions in the forces right now. If a woman wishes to take a position which potentially could be combat related, she should be able to have that opportunity as well.
For many, many years people who trained for combat, in fact, functioned in the Armed Forces in peacetime conditions. They have to be prepared for combat, that is part of the job. They have to demonstrate their capacity for leadership, their courage, their ability to be promoted by what they do in both combat and non-combat roles.
When you deny women access to 70,000 positions in our Armed Forces, and that is some 70 per cent of the positions, which is the situation today, effectively they have nothing approaching equal rights in the Armed Forces of Canada.
If women were treated as individuals, you would then get a situation where a woman who was particularly tough, strong,
June 2, 1986

aggressive and motivated might decide that she wished to go into a combat role. Likewise, you might find a male in the forces who, perhaps, with other characteristics, wished to qualify as a cook or as a personnel officer or in some other position that perhaps was not related. The situation now is that women fill 25 per cent of the positions in the forces for which they are permitted to compete. We are creating, in other words, a job ghetto for women because before very long women will have filled all of the positions open to them and then they will no longer be able to increase their participation in the forces at all.
I would remind Hon. Members that in the RCMP where officers must constantly face the risk of danger, of violence on the part of criminals, we make no such distinction between women and men. Women officers take the same roles as males and, therefore, run the same risks of violence or injury as male officers in the RCMP. That is also true of women in the provincial and municipal police forces up and down this country. I would remind Hon. Members that there is no nuclear free zone in Canada where women might be hurt by the fall of a nuclear bomb. Therefore, as far as peacetime exposure to injury as a result of violent combat is concern, women are as vulnerable as men and civilians within Canada.
It seems to me that what is occurring here is that the Government is going to go along with the prejudices of people who are already in the Forces. The analogy has been given of the resistance of the American forces, perhaps ours too, to the integration of blacks into those forces after and during the Second World War. That was difficult at the time. It may be difficult to integrate women into certain roles in the Armed Forces today. Nonetheless, their success in the Armed Forces, and the fact that they are a relatively high proportion as compared to other Armed Forces indicate that this country has been a pace setter. Therefore, I ask why we must stop being a pace setter when it comes to giving equality rights to women in the Armed Forces of this country?
I suggest that the resolution put forward by my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), is strong and positive. It has already been endorsed by Members from all Parties who have studied this issue closely. I would ask that all Parties support this resolution and allow it to become the declared policy of the House and of the Parliament of Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EQUALITY RIGHTS ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING SUBCOMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), my colleague on the Justice and Solicitor General Committee. I am also pleased to speak as a result of my experience as a member of the former Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. During our cross-country hearings last fall, when we went from one end of the country to the other, we had occasion not only to hear witnesses speak to the issue before our committee, we had occasion to visit a number of military bases in Canada as well as NORAD bases in the United States.
Equality Rights
From time to time, as part of the informal meetings with military personnel at those bases, I would ask both male and female members of the Armed Forces about this issue of women in combat roles. Frankly, I was surprised by the unanimity of opinion that was very much against any change in the status quo.
Therefore, I think it is important that we in the House examine the history and present status of women in combat roles in other jurisdictions when considering this motion.
The only modern experience of women being employed in combat in war was in the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia with the partisans during the Second World War and in Israel in the late forties. In all three cases, we were talking about a defensive situation. There was an enemy in the homeland and an over-all shortage of people to face that enemy.
In the case of Israel in 1948, women were withdrawn from combat after only three weeks. At the end of hostilities, the other countries withdrew women from combat without explanation, and that restriction still stands.

Today in the Soviet Union it is estimated that women make up less than .5 per cent of the armed forces, all in non-combat roles.

Armed Forces throughout the world, without meaningful exception, do not employ women in combat roles. Belgium, the Netherlands and Norway are the only three countries in the world known to profess unlimited employment of women in their Armed Forces. The percentages of women in the Armed Forces in these countries, interestingly enough, are respectively only 3.8 per cent, 1.4 per cent, and 1.2 per cent. These countries maintain their Armed Forces with compulsory military service, but, paradoxically, this conscription applies only to men. In June, 1985, in all three of those countries, there were only 18 to 30 women in what the Canadian forces would classify as combat occupations. Another 65 or so were serving with combat units but in non-combat occupations such as radar operators with artillery units.
Studies are presently under way in our country to determine the standards for performance of duties within each military occupation. These tests, and data from other Armed Forces, indicate that about 90 per cent of male applicants meet the most demanding physical requirements for combat, but that only about 2 per cent of women applicants would qualify physically. If women were required to serve in all areas of the Armed Forces, it would be necessary to impose gender-free physical selection standards on all members since both men and women would have to perform all of the military tasks in the Canadian Armed Forces, including the most physically demanding. While gender-free physical selection standards would broaden the scope of roles for women who could meet these higher standards, it would certainly result in a military career being denied to the majority of Canadian women.

June 2, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Under these circumstances, it is estimated that the total number of women in the forces would decrease by up to 75 per cent. This estimate is consistent with the data from Belgium, Holland and Norway, which have only about a quarter of the proportion of women in their Armed Forces that Canada has.
As other Members have indicated during this debate, the push-button war concept is a fallacy. Modern technology has not reduced the physical demands of warfare. In fact, in many ways those demands have been increased. Strength and endurance are more important than ever and medical information indicates that there are significant differences between genders in physical endurance and body strength. Thus, it would be difficult for most women to meet the physical standard requirements for duty in combat units.
Today, the modern soldier may be transported more quickly to his operational zone, but once there he must physically operate a wide range of weapons unheard of in former wars. As well, he must carry equipment that would enable combat operations to continue throughout hours of darkness, resulting in sustained high intensity operations with little respite. There were many cases in the Falklands where the ability to endure prolonged physical stress placed victory within grasp.
There are many non-combat trades which serve in combat units. Everyone must be able to perform the most physically demanding tasks. As the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) pointed out earlier this afternoon, the Falklands campaign showed the devastating effect of modern missiles. These missiles caused unexpectedly serious damage, which, in turn, increased the physical demands on the crews who had to deal with damage control. Every sailor, regardless of his trade, had to be physically able to contribute to the ship's survival. Operational effectiveness must remain the primary consideration in military personnel management. Failure to perform these physically demanding tasks could result in the loss of the ship and the lives of the entire crew.
There is no indication of significant interest from women for service in combat roles. Applicants have been a rarity. As I indicated in my opening remarks, women now in the forces demonstrate little desire for transfer to combat units. Women who served in non-combat field trials were unanimous in concluding that women should not serve in combat. As well, it should be noted that no witnesses who appeared before the Equality Rights Subcommittee did so to seek entry to a combat role for themselves.
Having said that, I want to address the motion of the Hon. Member and say that I personally have difficulty in supporting paragraph 1 of his proposal for the reasons I have outlined. However, I have no difficulty in supporting the second paragraph which calls for the employment and promotion practices of the Canadian Armed Forces to be monitored by the Canadian Human Rights Commission and that progress in revising policy in the manner recommended by the committee be evaluated by the commission at regular intervals.

subtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-PROFITS OF WHEAT MILLERS
CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-PROFITS OF WHEAT MILLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are well aware, my constituency is an urban one. It is a constituency which one might describe as being located in the geographic heart of Metropolitan Toronto. Therefore, it is not a constituency in which there are farms or rural areas. Having said that, I want to make it quite clear that I and my constituents have a great deal of sympathy for the present-day plight of Canadian farmers. We are only too well aware of the great problems facing Canadian farmers and we understand, for instance, that western Canadian wheat farmers, in particular, but also Ontario wheat farmers, have to compete in the international wheat market with producers of wheat around the world, particularly producers of wheat in Europe and in the United States. We understand as well that the Europeans and the Americans subsidize their wheat. We know that as a result of those subsidies and that competition, the world price of wheat has fallen to something like $3.54 a bushel, which is approximately the price of wheat in 1974.
We know as well, and we have heard many times from Canadian western farmers, that the price of $3.54 a bushel does not cover their production costs. It is no wonder, then, we have farm bankruptcies of a very substantial nature. Understanding all these things, we sympathize as consumers and urban dwellers with the plight of the western farmers and believe there must be some aid and assistance for western farmers.
Having said that, I want to ensure that you, Mr. Speaker, and other Members of the House, understand that I and my constituents, as consumers, are also concerned about what impact aid for farmers may have on the consumers. We have just gone through a period of very substantial inflation. It seems to be over for the moment, thank goodness, but it was in the double digit range for quite some time, in fact, two or three years. Inflation is now below 4 per cent. It is a more stable inflation than at any time since 1971. However, when my constituents go to the stores, they find that prices are still going up. It is not a question of prices rising at the same rate as before. They do not go up every day the way they once did. However, there is still an inflation rate and prices are still rising.
Those price increases impact most severely on people with very modest incomes. My constituency is one in which the income levels range from one end of the scale to the other. I have a quite substantial number of very modest income earners in my constituency, so it is of particular concern that the price increases impact on people with small and modest incomes more severely than they do on others. It is also of particular concern that increases in the price of staple products, such as bread and white flour, impact most severely on those people with modest incomes. That is because they do not have a discretionary income which they can choose to spend or not spend on staple items.
Adjournment Debate
Having said all of that, we still understand and share the concerns of our western farm neighbours with the plight of raising wheat and trying to sell it at a lower cost than the cost of production. However, some of the suggested solutions cause us concern because we know that if we raise the domestic price of wheat, as has been suggested as a solution to the farmers' problems, that will impact on us as consumers, particularly because of the import restrictions on foreign flour imported into Canada. Because of those restrictions, the international price of wheat and flour cannot have any moderating effect on domestic prices in Canada.
As well, we have heard comments from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which assures us that a modest price increase in the domestic price of wheat will not impact severely on the price of a loaf of bread. In fact, it says that a $1 per bushel increase will mean only a 1.5 cent-increase on a 24-ounce loaf of bread and that a $3 per bushel increase will mean a less than 5-cent increase on a 24-ounce loaf of bread. At the same time, we also hear from the bakers that that will not be the case. They say that if the price of a bushel of wheat goes up by $1, it will cost almost five cents more to buy a loaf of bread and, if the cost of a bushel of wheat goes up by $3, it will cost some 15 cents more to buy a loaf of bread. There is a difference between the story we are hearing from the wheat farmers and the story we are hearing from the millers and bakers.
What is the reason for that difference? What is the answer? Obviously the answer is the middlemen, including the brokers, millers, bakers and retailers. We have a number of concerns about the middlemen. There are only a limited number of these people and, therefore, there is corporate concentration. There is a lack of competition in this area and that is reflected by the fact that Canadian millers' profits are 7.6 per cent of sales while U.S. millers' profits are only 1.8 per cent of sales. As well, we are concerned with the fact that when the price of wheat goes up, charges for middlemen increase on a percentage basis and not a flat rate basis. That may have been satisfactory in the past, but it is not satisfactory at the present time. You and I, Mr. Speaker, know that in many cases lawyers have had to give up percentage charges in favour of flat rates. It seems to me it is time the middlemen between the producers of wheat and the consumers of wheat do that as well.
I think there are answers to this problem. For instance, a special committee that is now studying the matter has before it an array of things that may be done. It may place controls on the situation, but there has to be an answer, and I am looking for that answer from the Parliamentary Secretary. I am looking for an answer that is fair to farmers but at the same time will not gouge consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
June 2, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Speaker, as the Hon. Member is aware, a special parliamentary committee has been appointed to consider wheat pricing. This committee is holding public hearings across the country at the moment. I would like to take this opportunity to urge interested citizens to make their views on possible impacts known to the committee and Members of Parliament.
The report of the committee is due on June 6, only a few days away, and I would not wish to prejudge the outcome of the very thorough investigation now being undertaken. Nevertheless, some very general comments on the issues raised by the Hon. Member's question are perhaps in order at this time.
The cost of raw materials has a limited weight in determining the final retail price of wheat-using products. The cost of flour itself has been estimated to be only 70 per cent of the value of bakery products, 8 per cent of biscuits, 30 per cent of dry pasta and prepared flour products, and only 5 per cent of breakfast cereals. However, due to the mark-up policies at each stage of production, price increases at the farmer level in certain circumstances can be passed on and exacerbated as they move through the processing retail chain. It is important for consumers, particularly low-income earners who are higher consumers of bread and cereals, that mark-ups be kept to reasonable levels. I am pleased the Hon. Member is conscious of that fact. It is also in the interests of wheat-using industries themselves which must compete in domestic and international markets.
The particular study which the Hon. Member quoted referred to the existence of a problem of concentration and hence excessive profit taking in the milling industry. It is my information that the data used in that study may not have been appropriate for this type of financial analysis and that consequently the level of profits in the Canadian industry may have been substantially overstated. Analysis undertaken on the basis of alternate data is available. It indicates profit levels in the milling industry which appeared to be much more in keeping with the rest of the food industry as a whole.
The Director of Investigation and Research under the Combines Investigation Act is also aware of the reports concerning profit levels in the milling industry. He will look into any information that its performance reflects conduct contrary to the provisions of the Act. I am confident that any Member of the House who receives information of such conduct in the flour milling industry would bring it immediately to the attention of the director.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-MONITORING OF EXAMINATION OF TASK FORCE OPTIONS.
GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-MONITORING OF EXAMINATION OF TASK FORCE OPTIONS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 28, 1986, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) a question regarding Government expenditures and, in particular, how the process of examining the Nielsen task force options and recommendations would be monitored. After all, a
colossal amount of work was put into that project and it is essential that we reap the benefits.
The Nielsen task force, initiated on September 18, 1984, faced a gargantuan task in reviewing 989 programs and services in the federal Government, reflecting annual expenditures of more than $92 billion, including tax expenditures. Despite the complexity of its task, the task force had one year in which to complete its mandate. The huge report, tabled in the House on March 11, 1986, was the first ever attempt to present a comprehensive overview of what the federal Government actually does.
One of the most interesting elements of the study team report was that each team, whatever program area it was examining, identified several broad patterns which recurred frequently. These generic issues, as the report identified them, offer an interesting and at times rather disheartening view of how the federal Government has worked to date. The universal subsidy is a recurring theme in the study team reports, that is, subsidies through both tax provisions and direct expenditures. The study teams found that many subsidies were not warranted on economic grounds, aside from political considerations.
Another problem the study teams identified in respect of universal subsidy was that a vast array of Government programs had been developed which subsidized effort rather than success. Another generic issue identified by the study teams dealt with what they called the fiscal totality; in other words, a comprehensive overview of the total impact of expenditures.
New program proposals have not been examined within the broader context of Government expenditure. Therefore, government spending expands exponentially as new programs are added to old, and it becomes well nigh impossible to determine the precise financial interrelationships of new programs and old programs. I think these programs need some sunset provisions.
This has contributed to the view that government spending was out of control. Closely related to this lack of comprehensive overview of government programs and their impact is the lack of institutional memory. This can result in unnecessary duplication of programs and efforts and programs continuing after their usefulness has passed.
The study teams also identified other generic issues, such as inadequate program evaluation, shortcomings in the personnel system which provide few incentives to reduce organization size, and the pervasive force of the status quo. In all, the study teams identified issues which are pervasive throughout the federal Government and which seriously need addressing. The prevalence of subsidies and programs which reward effort rather than success is another element in federal programs areas which requires action.
The Nielsen task force has done a fine job on a difficult and complex task within a very short time frame. Not only did it identify specific program areas where changes can be affected,
June 2, 1986

but it identified the broader themes which underlie the specifics and which cannot be addressed by just one department, but which need the commitment of the whole Government to bring about the substantial changes in attitude and profit so desperately required to make the federal Government's programs and programs delivery more efficient, more effective and more responsive to the people of this country.
Some specific findings of the study teams, in addition to the more pervasive issues, included procurement. The study team noted that the federal Government spends more than $9 billion a year on procurement. This study team concluded that the Government can "spend smarter" by better managing the system currently in place and by increasing competitive tendering and promoting contracting out initiatives. The study team which examined services and subsidies to business subtitled their report "giving with both hands". This refers to an overly rich, overlapping industrial incentive program. This study team undertook 140 program reviews, encompassing 218 separate federal programs costing $16.4 billion in 1984-85, and involving more than 68,000 public servants.
The study team found that this incentive program needed rationalizing to allow Government input to be better targeted and to require sufficient private sector input. For example, federal assistance for any private investment from tax expenditures, ERDAs and grants should not exceed 50 per cent of a project's cost. These are just two of the hundreds of program areas examined by the study teams.
The many recommendations and options put forward by the task force deserve serious examination. The appropriate standing committees will be examining these options and, indeed, the Government had put into effect some recommendations prior to the publication of the full report. It is vital, however, now that we have a comprehensive overview of government programs, that the examination of the recommendations be monitored correctly, that the appropriate changes, especially with regard to the pervasive attitudinal ones, be made as quickly as possible. This should be done in order to improve services to the public, promote more efficient management, lighten the burden of bureaucratic regulations on all of us and, most important, lighten the load of the taxpayers in Canada who are sick and tired of a high taxation level on the one hand and poor programs on the other.
While I commend the efforts of everyone involved in this task force, I now strongly urge the respective committees to get on with dealing with those substantial recommendations and options so that we can save the people hundreds of millions in tax dollars.

tabled by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) and his team last March 11, as you know.
When tabling the 20 studies the Deputy Prime Minister had given-and the House followed that recommendation: each study was referred to the appropriate standing committee of the House. So the report on the study on agriculture was referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture- transport, finance, consumer and corporate affairs, forests, environment, culture, and so forth. As you know, Mr. Speaker, each standing committee will hear witnesses, consider the studies in question, and eventually table in the House its major conclusions on the study.
A number of committees, including that of Agriculture, have already started and, as you know, each House Standing Committee has its own working schedule. It is the committee itself which will decide when it will hear the various witnesses, and on what it will report to the House of Commons later on.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is marvelous. It was part of the program which the Government had in mind, when elected on September 4, 1984, to make sure that all Members of the House are involved in the decision making process of all the policies involving Canada nationally.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for a particular dossier is only one of many parties involved and will have to follow the procedure established and the decisions made by the Standing Committee.
Mr. Speaker, I think therefore that we should be satisfied with the work that will be made by each of the Standing Committees, following the 20 studies tabled, and by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. I am sure that the Committee will make proper and timely decisions and then report to the House, and that both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and its Department will consider the various recommendations with utmost interest.

subtopic: REFUGEES-NEW DETERMINATION PROCESS. (fl) PORTUGUESE VISAS INQUIRY
REFUGEES-NEW DETERMINATION PROCESS. (fl) PORTUGUESE VISAS INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to pursue in this adjournment debate a question which I asked of the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean) on May 22, the day immediately following his announcement on the refugee determination process which he plans to establish. The Minister's announcement was followed by immediate criticism from the community.
I feel that the Minister and the Government betrayed the constituency, which led to the consultative process on the evaluation and establishment of a new refugee determination process. The failure was largely in three monumental areas. The first was the right of legal counsel to refugee claimants, the second on the question of universal accessibility which

June 2, 1986
Adjournment Debate
should exist for all refugees, and the third was the failure to provide a strong, effective and specialized appeal body.
On the weekend immediately following the announcement by the Minister in Toronto, the Standing Conference of Canadian Organizations Concerned for Refugees, which represents about 100 organization across the country, met to discuss the new policy. They passed a resolution which declared "non-confidence in the Government for its failure to respect the fundamental principles unanimously recommended by non-governmental groups across Canada-and for its failure to adhere to the rule of law as required by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms." The Standing Conference in Toronto was an example and a reflection of how most of the organizations, and indeed the Liberal Party, reacted to the question of the new refugee determination process.
On May 22 I asked the Minister specifically to give us his assurance and the assurance of his Government that these three areas which failed miserably to address the fairness and effectiveness in the system would be looked at once again in preparation for the legislation which the Minister intends to table in the House in the fall. Rather than having an arduous debate in the House and the country, we feel that these elements, which are nearly unanimously agreed to by the organizations, service clubs and churches serving the refugees, should be incorporated in the legislation before the Minister introduces it in order that it will be relevant and will be approved more quickly than it would be if a prolonged debate were required.
I want to speak briefly on three issues, the first being the right to legal counsel. At present the policy announced by the Minister is silent on this question. Nowhere in his statement or briefing notes does the principle become evident. There is a lot of concern and there has been a lot of criticism over the fact that presently a claimant does not have the right to legal counsel from the initial stages. This is wrong. It flies in the face of the Charter of Rights and our judicial system.
It is inconceivable that individual claimants can have used against them information they have given to immigration officers without the benefit of legal counsel. It was recommended by those groups which appeared before the standing committee that a claimant have the right to legal counsel from the beginning. The claimant would pay for counsel, but he or she had to have legal counsel available.
The second issue concerned the appeal procedure. The Minister recommended that the Federal Court of Appeal be the body of appeal. However, the Minister knows very well that the Federal Court lacks expertise in refugee law and an understanding of the situation in individual countries. As well, the mandate of the court precludes it from receiving new evidence, or reassessing the individual involved. In addition, the Federal Court of Appeal looks only at perhaps 7 per cent to 8 per cent of all cases. That is a minute number, and most of them end up being paper decisions. The Liberal Party, along
with other organizations, has called for a specialized refugee appeal board so that the individuals concerned might have the benefit of the doubt. If we do make a mistake, we would not be sending the individual back to the country where he was persecuted. Rather, we would have a specialized board to deal with the situation in a very humane way.
The last point deals with accessibility. Universal accessibility does not exist, and we hope the Minister will address that point as well as the others I have raised. I notice you are telling me that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I look forward to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister assuring this House and the community at large that this review will take place and be reflected in legislation.

subtopic: REFUGEES-NEW DETERMINATION PROCESS. (fl) PORTUGUESE VISAS INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to deal with a subject which differs slightly from those with which I deal usually. If I may, before I address directly the issue raised by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), I should like to point out that in its remarks, he mentioned that the Liberal Party of Canada had made a number of recommendations, done this or that over the past two years. If only the Liberal Party of Canada, while in power, had done something about this issue, it might not have today to take its current position.
Mr. Speaker, the right to counsel is already provided for under the current procedure for claiming refugee status and will be reconfirmed in the legislation dealing with the new refugee determination process. This is a matter that is more concerned with immigration procedures than with recognition of refugee status. The point the Hon. Member for York West is concerned about is the right to counsel at a secondary examination, that is, before the inquiry. The Hon. Member is concerned about having counsel present at the examination at port of entry, which examination is aimed at determining, for Immigration purposes, the eligibility of any person seeking to enter Canada. At this stage no counsel is permitted to be present, since claimants are sent all the information collected at that time so they can tell their side of the story if the information is used against them at the Immigration inquiry.
The matter of unrestricted access to a hearing did not meet with unanimous consent. However, nearly all observers agreed that matters of credibility should be assessed at the end of a hearing by the adjudicator. However, we have no obligation to allow access to individuals who do not require protection and when there is no need to evaluate the facts on their credibility. Two of the proposed restrictions on access-in the case of individuals who submit the same claim again and those who are under a removal order-are now in effect as part of an access system that is considered to be universal. The two other restrictions would apply to individuals who have exceeded the prescribed period or are already protected by another country. These criteria can be applied objectively on the basis of documentary evidence. However, there is provision for hearing these claims in cases where the situation changes. In addition, the right of access to the new refugee determination process
June 2, 1986

will be explicitly provided in the legislation for people arriving at entry points and who might need Canadian protection.
In its fifth report, Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration concluded that a second review of the merits of the application is not necessary. The superior quality of the hearing on the merits of the application, a hearing generally favourable to the claimant, makes a second review redundant. Instead, any person whose application is rejected by the refugee determination committee will have the right, if so authorized, to appeal to the Federal Court of Canada. Mr. Speaker, quality rather than quantity ensures fairness.
The current process does not work out well precisely because it provides for too many review levels. The proposed process will be far superior to the current practice and will be second to none worldwide. In addition provisions are made to re-open the case of people whose situation has changed. Finally, we must keep in mind that this refugee determination process will not be the only recourse available. This process has been established to take into consideration the generous provisions concerning the special re-examination of cases for humanitarian reasons, and Canada's policy is not to deport applicants to countries which are experiencing serious troubles or which violate human rights.
Adjournment Debate
Finally, as concerns visas for the Portuguese, a decision to remove the dispensation from a visitor's visa in the case of Portuguese citizens must not be taken lightly. The requirement for a visa is imposed only when we are convinced that there is no other solution.
After careful study of this problem with members of Cabinet and representatives of the Portuguese community, it was decided that it would not be appropriate to require a visa for the moment. There is no need for the Government to apologize for action which was never taken. Following discussions with representatives of the Portuguese community, a pilot project was implemented to help the immigrants to become more familiar with the process and reduce the risk of exploitation. The Government will continue to monitor the situation closely and will take other action if required to put an end to the abusive utilization of the refugee determination process. Thank you for your understanding, Mr. Speaker.
